LLM · RAG · Text-to-SQL Featured

FloatChat: Conversational Access to ARGO Ocean Data

Based on Smart India Hackathon 2025 problem statement SIH25040, Ministry of Earth Sciences

Ask questions about Indian Ocean ARGO float data in plain English. A router sends each question either to cited retrieval over generated float and region summaries, or to text-to-SQL that is validated and run as a read-only database user. Every answer shows its evidence (route, SQL, rows, chart, citations), and questions the data cannot answer are refused instead of invented. Everything runs on a local open-weights model.

  • Four layers of SQL safety: scope gate, 14-rule validator, read-only Postgres role and a 5 s statement timeout, plus deterministic answer checks that drive one targeted repair attempt.
  • OpenTelemetry traces exposed a silent bug: Ollama's default 4,096-token window was cutting off a roughly 4,165-token prompt. Fixed with num_ctx 6144 on every call and a guard test.
  • Separate evaluation harnesses for retrieval, generation and SQL, plus a McNemar A/B test. The README reports failures and retractions, not just wins.
  • Ingests real NetCDF data (corrected values, QC flags) into PostgreSQL with PostGIS sea polygons: 80 floats, 1,099 profiles, 175,364 measurements, plus 187 drifting buoys.
Design notes and limits

Honest numbers: SQL accuracy is from a single run and can move by about 0.1 between runs; window-function questions are still weak (2 of 6).

Trade-offs: median about 38 s per SQL question on a laptop CPU, at zero API cost. Not deployed to the cloud by choice; CI builds and pushes Docker images to GHCR.

Daily Temperature Forecasting

A production-style MLOps microservice that predicts tomorrow's minimum temperature from the previous 30 days. The model is deliberately simple; the engineering around it is the point: a reproducible pipeline, leakage-safe features, train/serve parity, gated CI/CD and drift monitoring.

2.147°C
Test RMSE on the last 724 days
~13%
Lower RMSE than persistence (2.478°C)
Exact
Metrics reproduced by dvc repro
  • Leakage-safe features (rolling windows end yesterday) and a chronological train/test split with no shuffling.
  • Protected main: PRs need green CI (ruff, black, pytest). CD pushes images to GHCR, and Render only switches traffic after /health passes.
  • Prometheus metrics, MLflow experiment tracking and an Evidently drift report. No secrets in the repo.
Design notes and limits

Scope: trained on Melbourne data (1981 to 1990), so it is Melbourne-only; a random forest cannot extrapolate to hotter climates. The web page still lets you try any place via Open-Meteo.

Hosting: Render free tier, so the first request after idle can take a minute to wake up.

Machine Learning · Classification Complete · runs locally

Telco Customer Churn Prediction

A calibrated XGBoost classifier that flags telecom customers likely to leave. The decision threshold is chosen by minimising business cost instead of using the default 0.5, and a Streamlit form shows the churn probability, a risk verdict and the expected cost of acting versus not acting.

0.944
Churn recall on test (353 of 374 churners)
0.836
Test ROC-AUC
0.140
Brier score (calibrated)
  • Found and fixed data leakage in my original notebook: encoding and SMOTE ran before cross-validation and inflated fold scores from about 0.72 to 0.90. Both now run inside the pipeline, per fold.
  • Cost-based threshold (missed churner 780 vs wasted offer 65) picked on validation at 0.08, matching the theoretical 0.077. The test split is touched once.
  • Model, threshold and feature order ship in one artifact, so the app cannot drift from training.
Design notes and limits

Trade-off: catching 94% of churners costs precision (0.40). That is intended when a missed churner costs 12 times more than an offer, and at 0.5 the test cost would be 2.7 times higher.

Caveat: the cost figures are assumptions, and the dataset is a static snapshot (IBM Telco, 7,043 customers).

LLM · RAG Complete · runs locally

Chat with Documents

Private question answering over your PDFs with page-level citations. PDF parsing, embeddings, vector search and the language model all run on your own machine, so documents never leave it. Rebuilt from an old LangChain tutorial into a framework-free, tested Python package.

0.80
Recall@5, frozen question set (0.87 after adjudication)
30
Hand-written questions on a 99-page manual
29
Tests in about 1 s, no model needed
  • Chunks never cross page boundaries, so every citation maps back to an exact file, page and similarity score.
  • Refuses instead of guessing: when retrieval is weak, the model says the documents do not contain the answer.
  • Tests use a fake embedder, a fake HTTP session and hand-built PDFs, so CI runs on Python 3.9 and 3.12 without torch or Ollama.
Design notes and limits

Evaluation: questions were written from the pages before any retrieval ran. Both the frozen and adjudicated scores are published so the correction is visible.

Next step: the misses are exact-identifier lookups and paraphrase gaps, which point to hybrid BM25 retrieval. No OCR yet for scanned PDFs.

TweetEval Sentiment Analysis

Four model families (TF-IDF with Logistic Regression, BiLSTM, BiGRU and RoBERTa) classify tweets as negative, neutral or positive. All are trained on the official TweetEval splits, scored with one shared metrics function and compared side by side in a Streamlit app.

0.599
Macro recall, TF-IDF + LR (official metric)
12,284
Tweets in the official test split
38
Tests with CI on every push
  • A tuned linear baseline beat both RNNs on test accuracy, while class weighting let the BiGRU catch 3,177 of 3,972 negative tweets versus 2,498 for LR.
  • Each model ships an inference_config.json, so the app always applies the preprocessing it was trained with.
  • New preprocessing is proven byte-identical to the old default by test, with emoticon handling added as an opt-in.
Design notes and limits

Honest gap: the committed RoBERTa weights started from a model already tuned on this task, so its score is not comparable and is not reported. A fair GPU retrain from a tweet-pretrained base is the next step.

Imbalance: only 16% of training tweets are negative, handled with balanced class weights.
